newsitem.title: USA: Veto threat on U.S. Senate intelligence bill.
newsitem.headline: Veto threat on U.S. Senate intelligence bill.

text.p: The White House threatened a veto Thursday of a Senate funding bill for intelligence activities on grounds it would intrude unconstitutionally on presidential power to control secret information.
In a statement of views, the Clinton administration expressed doubts about a provision to give information to relatives of Americans killed or kidnapped abroad.

It also faulted the bill for "elimination of core intelligence capabilities that are critical to satisfying high-priority national and military intelligence needs." It offered to work with senators to resolve funding issues.
Overall level of funds that would be authorised for the intelligence community in fiscal 1998 under the bill was secret.
The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence had no immediate comment on the veto threat. The bill was waiting a floor vote.
Committee members included a provision that federal employees could inform congressional authorities of wrongdoing without fear of reprisal even if the evidence involved classified data.

"This provision is clearly contrary to the Supreme Court's explicit recognition of the president's constitutional authority to protect national security and other privileged information" and was unconstitutional, the White House said.

"Congress may not vest lower-ranking personnel in the Executive Branch with a 'right' to furnish national security or other privileged information to a member of Congress without receiving official authorisation to do so," it said.

The section on release of information about murders and kidnapping needed the addition of language to ensure confidential information was protected and that investigations were not compromised, the White House said.
